facts.statement: Deinosuchus had a broad, alligator-like snout with a slightly bulbous tip.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus had an alligator-like, broad snout, with a slightly bulbous tip.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Deinosuchus contained 23 teeth in each maxilla.
facts.quote: Each maxilla (the main tooth-bearing bone in the upper jaw) contained 23 teeth.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Deinosuchus had at least 22 teeth in each dentary bone.
facts.quote: The tooth count for each dentary (tooth-bearing bone in the lower jaw) was at least 22.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus teeth were thick and robust, with rear teeth being short, rounded, and blunt.
facts.quote: All the teeth were very thick and robust; those close to the rear of the jaws were short, rounded, and blunt.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus teeth appear adapted for crushing rather than piercing.
facts.quote: They appear to have been adapted for crushing, rather than piercing.

facts.statement: The estimated bite force of Deinosuchus ranges from 18,000 N to 102,803 N.
facts.quote: The bite force of Deinosuchus has been estimated to be 18000 N to 102803 N.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus had a secondary bony palate allowing it to breathe while submerged.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus had a secondary bony palate, which would have permitted it to breathe through its nostrils while the rest of the head remained submerged underwater.

facts.statement: Osteoderms and connective tissue reinforced Deinosuchus's body to support it out of water.
facts.quote: Together, the osteoderms and connective tissue would have served as load-bearing reinforcement to support the massive body of Deinosuchus out of water.

facts.statement: Recent biomechanical analyses suggest Deinosuchus lacked the muscle force for an erect walk, limiting it to belly-dragging on land.
facts.quote: However, more recent analyses of the taxon's hindlimb biomechanics find that Deinosuchus would have run into issues generating enough muscular force to support its body and prevent the adoption of an erect-limbed "high walk" gait.

facts.statement: A 1999 estimate based on complete remains placed Deinosuchus size between 8 and 10 meters and weight between 2.5 and 5 metric tons.
facts.quote: Using more complete remains, it was estimated in 1999 that the size attained by specimens of Deinosuchus varied from 8 to 10 m with weights from 2.5 to 5 MT.

facts.statement: A Texas specimen with a 1.31 m skull suggested a total body length of 9.8 meters.
facts.quote: A reasonably well-preserved skull specimen discovered in Texas indicated the animal's head measured about 1.31 m, and its body length was estimated at 9.8 m.

facts.statement: A large D. riograndensis skull measured 147.5 cm in length.
facts.quote: A particularly large preserved skull from a D. riograndensis specimen was estimated to have come from an individual with a skull length of 147.5 cm.

facts.statement: Walter and colleagues suggested Purussaurus was larger than Deinosuchus.
facts.quote: They also suggested that Purussaurus would have been larger than Deinosuchus.

facts.statement: Colbert and Bird (1954) speculated Deinosuchus hunted and devoured contemporary dinosaurs.
facts.quote: In 1954, Edwin H. Colbert and Roland T. Bird speculated that Deinosuchus "may very well have hunted and devoured some of the dinosaurs with which it was contemporaneous".

facts.statement: Schwimmer (2002) proposed Deinosuchus fed on dinosaurs based on tooth marks on hadrosaurid vertebrae near Big Bend National Park.
facts.quote: David R. Schwimmer proposed in 2002 that several hadrosaurid tail vertebrae found near Big Bend National Park show evidence of Deinosuchus tooth marks, strengthening the hypothesis that Deinosuchus fed on dinosaurs in at least some instances.

facts.statement: Brochu (2003) agreed Deinosuchus probably ate ornithopods occasionally.
facts.quote: In 2003, Christopher A. Brochu agreed that Deinosuchus "probably dined on ornithopods from time to time."

facts.statement: Deinosuchus likely used ambush tactics similar to modern crocodilians to drown prey at the water's edge.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus is generally thought to have employed hunting tactics similar to those of modern crocodilians, ambushing dinosaurs and other terrestrial animals at the water's edge and then submerging them until they drowned.

facts.statement: A 2014 study suggested Deinosuchus could perform a "death roll" like modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: A 2014 study suggested that it would have been able to perform a "death roll", like modern crocodiles.

facts.statement: Schwimmer (2010) noted bite marks on a tyrannosauroid leg bone (NJSM 13096) from the Ellisdale Fossil Site.
facts.quote: A 2010 review by Schwimmer noted NJSM 13096, a tyrannosauroid (either an immature Appalachiosaurus or a Dryptosaurus) leg bone in the collection of the New Jersey State Museum recovered from the Ellisdale Fossil Site had bite marks on it.

facts.statement: Schwimmer and Williams (1996) proposed Deinosuchus preyed on marine turtles.
facts.quote: Schwimmer and G. Dent Williams proposed in 1996 that Deinosuchus may have preyed on marine turtles.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus likely used robust rear teeth to crush turtle shells.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus would probably have used the robust, flat teeth near the back of its jaws to crush the turtle shells.

facts.statement: Shells of the sea turtle Bothremys found in Deinosuchus's eastern habitat show bite marks likely from the crocodilian.
facts.quote: The "side-necked" sea turtle Bothremys was especially common in the eastern habitat of Deinosuchus, and several of its shells have been found with bite marks that were most likely inflicted by the giant crocodilian.

facts.statement: Smaller eastern North American Deinosuchus specimens were likely opportunistic feeders similar to modern American alligators.
facts.quote: The smaller Deinosuchus specimens of eastern North America would have been opportunistic feeders in an ecological niche similar to that of the modern American alligator.

facts.statement: Eastern North American Deinosuchus likely consumed marine turtles, large fish like Megalocoelacanthus, and young theropods.
facts.quote: They would have consumed marine turtles, large fish (such as Megalocoelacanthus), and smaller dinosaurs (including young theropods).

facts.statement: Larger Texas and Montana Deinosuchus were likely specialized hunters of dinosaurs like hadrosaurs, ceratopsians, and theropods.
facts.quote: The bigger, but less common, Deinosuchus that lived in Texas and Montana might have been more specialized hunters, capturing and eating dinosaurs (such as hadrosaurs, ceratopsians, and small and large theropods).

facts.statement: Schwimmer noted Deinosuchus was likely the apex predator in its eastern range as no theropods approached its size.
facts.quote: Schwimmer noted no theropod dinosaurs in Deinosuchus eastern range approached its size, indicating the massive crocodilian could have been the region's apex predator.

facts.statement: In 2002, Schwimmer questioned the validity of growth rate estimates, suggesting the osteodermal rings might reflect biannual cycles rather than annual ones.
facts.quote: Schwimmer noted in 2002 that Erickson and Brochu's assumptions about growth rates are only valid if the osteodermal rings reflect annual periods, as they do in modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: All known Deinosuchus specimens come from rocks dated to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: All known specimens of Deinosuchus were found in rocks dated to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The oldest Deinosuchus lived approximately 82 million years ago, and the youngest lived around 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: The oldest examples of this genus lived approximately 82 Ma, and the youngest lived around 73 Ma.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus was present on both sides of the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus was present on both sides of the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: In the Aguja Formation of Texas, where large specimens were found, Deinosuchus likely inhabited brackish-water bays.
facts.quote: In the Aguja Formation of Texas, where some of the largest specimens of Deinosuchus have been found, these massive predators probably inhabited brackish-water bays.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus is among the largest crocodilians of all time, with length estimates ranging from 8 to 15 meters and a maximum estimated weight of 9 tons.
facts.quote: Se encuentra entre los mayores crocodilianos de todos los tiempos; las estimaciones sobre su longitud varían de 8 a 15 metros y un peso máximo estimado de 9 toneladas.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus lived in North America (present-day US and northern Mexico) approximately 80 to 75 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Cretaceous Period.
facts.quote: Vivió en Norteamérica, lo que actualmente es Estados Unidos, y en lo que es el norte de México, hace aproximadamente entre 80 a 75 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en el Período Cretácico de la Era Mesozoica.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus was contemporary with dinosaurs and possibly fed on some species of them.
facts.quote: Fue contemporáneo de los dinosaurios y posiblemente se alimentaba de algunas especies de ellos.

facts.statement: In 1858, geologist Ebenezer Emmons described two large fossil teeth found in Bladen County, North Carolina.
facts.quote: En 1858, el geólogo Ebenezer Emmons describió dos grandes dientes fósiles hallados en el Condado de Bladen, en Carolina del Norte.

facts.statement: Although not initially recognized as such, the teeth described by Emmons were likely the first scientifically described remains of Deinosuchus.
facts.quote: Aunque no fueron inicialmente reconocidos como tales, estos dientes fueron probablemente los primeros restos descritos científicamente de Deinosuchus.

facts.statement: Another large tooth likely from Deinosuchus was discovered in Sampson County and named Polydectes biturgidus by Edward Drinker Cope in 1869.
facts.quote: Otro gran diente que probablemente provenía de un Deinosuchus fue descubierto en el cercano Condado de Sampson, siendo denominado Polydectes biturgidus por Edward Drinker Cope en 1869.

facts.statement: In 1903, John Bell Hatcher and T.W. Stanton discovered several fossil osteoderms lying on the surface of the ground in Willow Creek, Montana.
facts.quote: En 1903, en Willow Creek, Montana, se descubrieron varios osteodermos fósiles "yaciendo sobre la superficie del suelo" por John Bell Hatcher y T.W. Stanton.

facts.statement: W.J. Holland assigned the specimens to a new genus and species, Deinosuchus hatcheri, in 1909.
facts.quote: Holland asignó los especímenes a un nuevo género y especie, Deinosuchus hatcheri, en 1909.

facts.statement: A 1940 expedition by the American Museum of Natural History found more giant crocodilian fossils in Big Bend National Park, Texas.

facts.statement: These specimens were described by Edwin H. Colbert and Roland T. Bird in 1954 under the name Phobosuchus riograndensis.

facts.statement: Donald Baird and Jack Horner later assigned the Big Bend remains to Deinosuchus, a classification accepted by current researchers.

facts.statement: Despite its large size, Deinosuchus generally looked similar to modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus had a wide snout like an alligator with a slightly bulbous tip.

facts.statement: The upper jaw contained 21 or 22 teeth.
facts.quote: El maxilar (el hueso que abarca la mayoría de los dientes en la mandíbula superior) contenía 21 o 22 dientes.

facts.statement: All teeth were very thick and robust, while those near the back of the jaws were short, rounded, and blunt.

facts.statement: The teeth appear to have been adapted for crushing rather than cutting.
facts.quote: Estos parecen haber estado adaptados para aplastar, en vez de cortar.

facts.statement: When the jaw closed, only the fourth tooth of the lower jaw would have been visible.
facts.quote: Cuando la mandíbula se cerraba, solo el cuarto diente de la mandíbula inferior habría sido visible.

facts.statement: The osteoderms covering Deinosuchus's back were unusually large, heavy, and deeply pitted, with some being vaguely hemispherical in shape.
facts.quote: Los osteodermos (escudos óseos) que cubrían la espalda de Deinosuchus eran inusualmente grandes, pesados y con profundas fosas; algunos eran de una forma vagamente semiesférica.

facts.statement: The osteoderms and connective tissues may have served as a load-bearing support to hold Deinosuchus's massive body out of the water.
facts.quote: Los osteodermos y tejidos conectivos pudieron haber servido como un refuerzo de soporte de carga para soportar el enorme cuerpo de Deinosuchus fuera del agua.

facts.statement: Therefore, despite its bulk, Deinosuchus was probably almost as agile on land as its close relatives.
facts.quote: Por lo tanto, a pesar de su mole, Deinosuchus era probablemente casi tan ágil sobre tierra como sus parientes cercanos.

facts.statement: Deinosuchus had a bony secondary palate, which would have allowed it to breathe through its nostrils while the rest of its head remained submerged underwater.
facts.quote: Deinosuchus tenían un paladar secundario óseo, el cual le habría permitido respirar a través de sus fosas nasales mientras el resto de la cabeza permanecía sumergida bajo el agua.

facts.statement: The bite force of Deinosuchus has been estimated at more than 18,000 newtons.
facts.quote: La fuerza de mordida de Deinosuchus se ha estimado en más de 18000 newtons.

facts.statement: Biomechanical analyses of skull models suggest that Deinosuchus and Purussaurus may have been capable of performing the "death roll" maneuver used by modern crocodilians to subdue and dismember prey.
facts.quote: Análisis realizados con modelos biomecánicos de los cráneos de Sarcosuchus, Deinosuchus y Purussaurus han indicado que estos dos últimos pudieron haber sido capaces de realizar la maniobra conocida como "giro de la muerte", que es usada por los crocodilianos actuales para subyugar y desmembrar a sus presas.
